questions.stem: A master meets winds of Beaufort force 10 and no storm warning had been received. What does the Canada Shipping Act, 2001 (s. 112) require?
options: Give notice to vessels in the vicinity and to the prescribed authorities on shore
Nothing, because force 10 is only reportable for tropical storms
A report to the authorized representative within 30 days
Proceed to the nearest port and report there on arrival
questions.explanation: Section 112 requires the master of a Canadian vessel to give notice to vessels nearby and to authorities ashore when meeting winds of Beaufort 10 or more for which no storm warning was received. The 30-day report belongs to the TSB occurrence rule, and waiting until arrival defeats the point of a warning.

questions.stem: Which of these is NOT listed in s. 112 of the Canada Shipping Act, 2001 as a danger the master must warn others about?
options: Dangerous ice
A dangerous derelict
Subfreezing air temperatures with gale-force winds causing severe ice accretion
A forecast of fog for the next day
questions.explanation: Section 112 lists dangerous ice, a dangerous derelict or other direct danger to navigation, a tropical storm, Beaufort 10 or more with no storm warning, and severe ice accretion with subfreezing gale conditions. A fog forecast is a normal weather product, not a reportable danger.

questions.stem: Why are following and quartering seas a particular danger to a small vessel?
options: The waves always break over the bow first
The propeller comes out of the water in every following sea
Stability can be considerably reduced when the vessel travels at about the same speed and direction as the waves
The wind speed doubles when it comes from astern
questions.explanation: The FAO guide warns that stability can be considerably reduced when a vessel moves at about the speed and direction of the waves. The other statements are not what the guide says: waves overtaking from astern do not break over the bow, and the propeller does not always lift.

questions.stem: Running before a sea, the vessel begins to heel and yaw excessively. What does the guidance suggest first?
options: Speed up to outrun the waves
Slow down and/or change course
Hold course and speed and wait for the sea to calm
Lock the freeing ports shut
questions.explanation: FAO advice is to slow down or change course if heeling or yawing becomes excessive. Speeding up keeps the vessel on the wave, holding on does nothing about the problem, and freeing ports must stay free to drain water.

questions.stem: You are running a vessel into a harbour with a following sea. Which approach matches the FAO advice?
options: Match the speed of the waves, do not overtake the wave ahead, and do not let a breaker overtake you
Overtake each wave to cross the bar as quickly as possible
Stop and let breakers pass under the stern
Run at full speed to stay ahead of the breakers
questions.explanation: When running in, the advice is to match the wave speed, not overtake it and not let a breaker overtake the vessel. Racing ahead puts the vessel on the front of a wave where control is lost, and stopping lets breakers overtake it.

questions.stem: A large steep wave is about to overtake a small Coast Guard-type boat from astern. What does the Coast Guard guidance (TP 11637) advise?
options: Open the throttle to get ahead of the wave
Turn broadside to the wave to cut through it
Stop the engine and let the wave pass
Reduce speed sharply and point the bow into the wave
questions.explanation: TP 11637 advises sharply reducing speed and pointing the bow into an overtaking wave, because speed on the front of a big wave leads to loss of control. Turning broadside invites a broach, and stopping the engine leaves the boat without steerage.

options: The vessel is pushed broadside to the sea and rolls over
The vessel rolls steadily from side to side at its natural period
In extreme following seas the bow dives under the wave in front of the vessel
The vessel is held in place by an anchor in a swell
questions.explanation: TP 11637 says that in extreme cases a boat can pitchpole when the bow dives under a following wave. Being pushed broadside is broaching, and a steady roll or an anchor holding the bow is something else.

questions.stem: Which set of conditions all raise capsize risk for a small vessel?
options: Deep water, a rising tide, a following current, and daylight
Shallow water, a falling tide, a strong opposing current, towing and darkness
Calm seas, full fuel tanks, and a light load
Light wind, an empty deck, and a rising tide
questions.explanation: The Coast Guard guidance lists shallow water, a low or falling tide, a strong opposing current, towing, darkness, low fuel and water taken aboard as conditions that raise capsize risk. Calm water, a following current and daylight are not on the list.

questions.stem: A deckhand suggests locking the freeing port covers shut to stop water coming aboard in heavy weather. What is the right response?
options: Do not lock them: water on deck must drain quickly, and any locks must be easy to release
Lock them, because water on deck helps stability
Lock them only on the weather side
Remove the scuppers so that water drains faster
questions.explanation: FAO guidance says locking freeing port covers is dangerous because water trapped on deck must drain quickly; if locks are fitted the release should be easy to reach. Water on deck acts like free surface and cuts stability.

questions.stem: Ice has built up and the vessel has a list to starboard. Where do you start removing ice, and what else is advised?
options: From the higher (port) side first, to lift the starboard side
From the bow first, then the stern, whatever the list
From the freeing ports last, to keep weight low
From the lower (starboard) side first, and keep slack tanks to a minimum
questions.explanation: FAO advice is to remove ice from the lower side first and to keep slack tanks to a minimum. Clearing the high side first would raise the list. Freeing ports and scuppers should also be cleared of ice as soon as it forms.

questions.stem: Which item is part of the heavy-weather checklist in the Coast Guard guidance?
options: Remove the lifebuoys to avoid snagging
Open all hatches to ventilate
Rig lifelines and harnesses and secure loose gear and openings
Fill every slack tank with fuel
questions.explanation: The checklist covers securing loose gear and openings, lifelines and harnesses, protective clothing, engine room and fuel, charts and a crew briefing. Removing lifebuoys, opening hatches and filling slack tanks all go the wrong way.

questions.stem: The vessel's documented design limitation is wave heights up to 1 m. The forecast gives 2 m seas and a passenger trip is booked. Which rule applies?
options: The master may exceed the limitation if the passengers sign a waiver
No person may operate a passenger-carrying vessel in circumstances that exceed its design limitations (SVR s. 404(2))
Design limitations apply only to the builder, not to the operator
The limitation applies only when the vessel carries more than 12 passengers
questions.explanation: Section 404(2) of the Small Vessel Regulations forbids operating a passenger-carrying vessel under circumstances that exceed its design limitations. A waiver does not change the law, and the rule applies to the person operating the vessel.
